articles.text: After two years serving as Padre Grande of the Beach Dads Club, and more than six years attending the Pancake Breakfast with my family, I have learned that the secret ingredient behind this tradition is not the batter or the butter. It is the people and community partners who make it possible. I want to offer an equally heartfelt thank you to Village Market, Mulberry’s Market and Piedmont Grocery. Each has generously supported the Pancake Breakfast and helped make this tradition possible. Between commercial griddles, the Fun Zone, entertainment, equipment and other hard costs, the event simply would not remain affordable without the collective support of all three. They are not just vendors. They are community partners, and we are deeply grateful to each of them. One of the best pieces of advice I received came from my wife, Zeena Fakoury, who serves on the Piedmont Education Foundation board. She reminded me early on that the goal is not maximizing the profit margin. It is maximizing the fun factor. If the kids are excited and want to stay, parents have more time to mingle, connect and actually get to know one another. Dads end up standing shoulder to shoulder making it happen, and families leave wanting to return the following year. That is the win. A special thank you also belongs to Principal Anne Valva, whose energy and support have strengthened these events year after year. Beach is incredibly fortunate to have a leader who understands how much these shared experiences matter. And then there is the Fire Department, whose visits and genuine engagement with the kids these past few years can only be described as quite possibly the coolest thing to happen on a playground at 8 a.m. in a very long time. None of this happens without volunteers. For 21 years, generations of Beach dads have hauled equipment, mixed batter, worked the griddles and cleaned the playground. For me, being part of that tradition carries a deeper meaning. My daughter Dalia is now in fourth grade at Beach, and my son Zane is in sixth grade at Piedmont Middle School. By the time I entered sixth grade, I had already moved four times, with roughly a dozen more moves still ahead of me before eventually finding this community. I know how much it means to find a place that welcomes you and feels like home. Serving as Padre Grande has been one small way to give something back and help other new kids and families feel that same sense of belonging. So, whenever possible, please remember to start local. The businesses we support are often the same businesses quietly supporting our children, schools and traditions. And three cheers to the Beach Dads Club: the dads who built this tradition, the dads carrying it forward today and the next generation waiting to leave its own mark. Give a bunch of dads a few griddles, an early alarm and the full support of a community, and it turns out they can make a little magic on a playground. Thank you to Village Market, Mulberry’s Market and Piedmont Grocery, Principal Anne Valva, the Piedmont Fire Department and every volunteer who continues to show up. You are the secret ingredient behind the Pancake Breakfast, and we could not do it without you. –Rob Doebelin Padre Grande #20 & #21 Beach School Dads Club
articles.title: The secret ingredient of 21 years of pancakes

articles.text: Longtime Piedmont resident and conservation leader Cameron Wolfe will be honored by the Sonoma Botanical Garden (SBG) as its 2026 Gala Honoree & Legacy Leader at its annual gala in Glen Ellen, CA on October 3. Wolfe, who was a partner at the San Francisco office of Orrick, Herrington and Sutcliffe, LLP, became associated with Sonoma Botanical Garden in 2000, then named Quarryhill Botanical Garden, when the Garden’s visionary founder, Jane Davenport Jansen, passed away unexpectedly. Piedmont doyenne Helen Breck was on the Garden’s Board and recruited Wolfe to help the Garden weather legal matters related to Jansen’s death. Wolfe continued to provide pro bono legal services to the Garden and eventually served two 6-year terms on its Board and two years as the Board President. “Cameron stepped forward at a pivotal moment in the Garden’s history and has remained a steadfast champion for more than 25 years,” said Jeannie Perales, Executive Director, SBG. “His leadership, generosity, and commitment to conservation have helped the Garden endure and thrive. We are deeply grateful and proud to honor his remarkable legacy.” Wolfe is renowned for his volunteer efforts around Piedmont as well. He joined the Piedmont Recreation Committee in the late ‘60s and served two years as its Chair. In that role, he helped establish the Piedmont 4th of July Parade. He and his wife, Fran, organized Piedmont’s first Tree Lighting Ceremony in conjunction with the Piedmont Beautification Foundation. Most importantly, he secured the school-owned property at the corner of Hampton and LaSalle for the City of Piedmont and helped raise funds for the ballpark and playfield there. Wolfe has served on the Piedmont Education Foundation Board and the Piedmont Beautification Foundation where he continues to serve Cameron Wolfe, Jr. as an Advisor. Wolfe’s interest in the environment also led him to serve on the League to Save Lake Tahoe Board for 25 years. He and his wife Fran served as trustees for the Yosemite Fund for over 10 years. They are also long-time supporters of Save the Redwoods League and in 2012, Cameron commemorated a redwood grove in Pfeiffer Big Sur State Park to Fran – the Fran B. Wolfe Grove. The Gala will be held at the Sonoma Botanical Garden in Glen Ellen on October 3, 2026. Tickets and information are available at https://sonomabg.org/garden-gala-2026/. About Sonoma Botanical Garden Founded in 1987, Sonoma Botanical Garden (SBG) is a woodland experience where East meets West, celebrating the beauty and importance of Asian and California native plants. Nestled in the Sonoma Valley, the Garden’s 63 acres feature a unique Asian woodland, a California native oak savanna, and a Cabernet vineyard. Its mission is to inspire appreciation and understanding of Asian and California native plants and promote their conservation in natural habitats and gardens. Visit sonomabg.org for details. articles.text: Earlier this month, Patty Dunlap, President of the Piedmont Beautification Foundation (PBF), welcomed a full room of Trustees and advisors to the new board’s first meeting. Dunlap is serving her third year as President to help wrap up several projects underway before the next leadership change. Since the new Board took office on July 1, they’ve had a busy summer. The Spring Campaign for the Nature Play Area has proved extremely popular with Piedmonters, with donations crossing $70,000. Work is well underway at the Main Park Tot Lot, where the Nature Play Area will be installed, as well as the return of the swings. It is not too late to help make these projects a spectacular success, and additional contributions are very much appreciated. PBF is in its 62nd year of initiating and supporting projects for the safety, sustainability, and beautification of Piedmont. The organization has eight Trustees, three from the City of Piedmont, including the Mayor, the Vice Mayor, and the Chair of the Park Commission, and five from the Piedmont Garden Club. PBF has 29 advisors this year, including representatives from four other garden clubs in Piedmont: Hoe and Hope; Highlanders Garden Club; East Bay Garden Club and Home Gardeners. Measure GG The first item of business at the PBF meeting was consideration of the Measure GG Transfer Tax. Former Mayor Bob McBain, Chair of the Budget Advisory and Financial Planning Committee, explained the measure; the tax is a one-time tax applicable only to the transfer of real estate. The committee unanimously recommended a modest tax increase to bring Piedmont’s transfer tax more in line with those of other East Bay jurisdictions. After a thorough discussion of the proposal, the Trustees unanimously voted that PBF endorse the measure and recommend a YES vote on November 3. Bringing back a Piedmont tradition The other important item on the agenda was consideration of a principal focus for PBF’s Fall campaign. Nancy Kent, Piedmont’s Parks and Projects Manager, outlined several city needs, prompting Vice President Marilyn Weber to propose reviving PBF’s original Holiday Greeting Fund. Under the initiative, community members donate to PBF – honoring friends and neighbors – with proceeds funding city projects throughout the year. The Trustees unanimously approved the proposal. Details for the campaign will be highlighted in the Fall Brochure arriving this November. Donor names and accompanying tributes will be published in early 2027. People can make contributions to PBF at any time through the PBF website, PiedmontBeautificationFoundation.org. The committee unanimously recommended a modest tax increase to bring Piedmont’s transfer tax more in line with those of other East Bay jurisdictions. After a thorough discussion of the proposal, the Trustees unanimously voted that PBF endorse the measure and recommend a YES vote on November 3. Bringing back a Piedmont tradition The other important item on the agenda was consideration of a principal focus for PBF’s Fall campaign. Nancy Kent, Piedmont’s Parks and Projects Manager, outlined several city needs, prompting Vice President Marilyn Weber to propose reviving PBF’s original Holiday Greeting Fund. Under the initiative, community members donate to PBF – honoring friends and neighbors – with proceeds funding city projects throughout the year. The Trustees unanimously approved the proposal. articles.text: In November Piedmonters will vote to decide their next City Council members and decide on crucial measures that could impact the region. On the ballot is a transit tax measure called the Public Transit Revenue Measure, which would impose a sales tax for 14 years to fund public transportation systems in the region. At the Piedmont City Council meeting on September 8, AC Transit representatives discussed the potential impacts if the measure fails to pass and the current financial struggles that AC Transit is facing. AC Transit covers 364 square miles, and serves more than three million riders monthly, in 13 cities and eight unincorporated communities in Alameda and Contra Costa counties. According to Ryan Lau, the External Affairs representative at AC Transit, their costs have risen, and their revenue has flattened, causing a budget deficit. “When the cost of running our bus network rises faster than the revenue supporting it, it results in a fiscal cliff,” said Lau. “Our regional sales tax revenue has flattened, and our fare revenue growth has slowed. At the same time, fuel costs have gone up by 28%. Bus maintenance parts have increased by 14%, and the cost of buying new buses has surged by 35%.” With the increased costs, AC Transit is reportedly operating at a budget deficit. Over the next four years, AC Transit faces a $200 million deficit, which is roughly $50 million a year beginning in 2027. “Without a long-term sustainable funding source, we’re looking at service reductions of up to 16%, and those are unavoidable. We’re also looking at potential human costs, with layoffs projected to affect up to 300 employees,” said Lau. Piedmont would see service reductions to Lines 12, 18, 88, P, and V. The service reductions include reducing frequency to 30 minutes on weekdays and hours of operation from 6 a.m. to 10 p.m. The Transbay lines P and V would face reductions in westbound morning trips and eastbound afternoon trips. These reductions would go into effect if the transit tax measure in November does not pass. If approved by voters, the measure would impose a transit sales tax of 1.0% in San Francisco and 0.5% in Alameda, Contra Costa, San Mateo, and Santa Clara counties. It would generate an estimated $980 million annually for Bay Area buses, trains, and ferries. AC Transit’s share would be $52 million a year. This would help protect the existing bus services and prevent layoffs. “If the ballot measure fails, there are going to be a tremendous number of unexpected consequences,” said Paul Kincaid, Assistant General Manager of AC Transit. “This contingency service plan is the best that we can do right now, and we hope that we will be able to throw it in the trash come November.” AC Transit is hosting a public hearing on October 14 at 2 p.m. and 6 p.m. Bay Area residents can give formal public comment on all of AC Transit’s proposed plans. Residents can submit comments through email, phone, or mail. All of AC Transit’s contact information can be found on its website, along with its contingency plan at https://www.actransit.org/contingency-plan.

articles.text: The California State Board of Education (SBE) has started accepting applications for its 2027-28 Student Board Member for current juniors. The chosen student will debate and vote on statewide education policies that directly affect millions of students across the state. A California public high school student has been selected to serve a one-year term on the State Board of Education every year since 1969. The role will require the person to attend bi-monthly meetings in Sacramento. Hotel and meals are completely covered, plus the representative will earn a $100 daily stipend. The term runs from August 1, 2027 to July 31, 2028. The representative will attend roughly six 2-day board meetings across the state over the course of the year. The application package is on the State Board of Education Student Member Recruitment Page at Cde.ca.gov/be/ms/mm/sbestudentmember.asp Completed applications must be turned in by Friday, September 25, 2026, at 5:00 p.m. Email completed application packages to sbe@sbe.ca.gov or submit it directly via the SBE Online Portal.

articles.text: At the September 9 School Board meeting the board announced progress in the search for a new, permanent superintendent. Following a request for proposal for search firms the board received four applications and has selected Leadership Associates to conduct the search. Leadership Associates conducted the search four years ago which led to the hiring of Jennifer Hawn. Interim Superintendent Donald Evans will lead the search. School Board President Ruchi Medhekar noted that Leadership was chosen for their network and their experience in California. “A reason why California experience specifically was important was because the rules in California are very nuanced and different. The way that we do our budgeting is nuanced,” said Medhekar. The board hopes to announce a new superintendent by December 9 with the first day on the job starting January 1, 2027. “As a reminder, when we did this the last time around there was a whole phase with community input, surveying, meetings. That’s all going to happen again. There’s a timeline for that,” explained board Vice President Michael Malione. Interim Superintendent Donald Evans confirmed that he will be in charge until the new person is found. “I will be here until the new superintendent starts. The last superintendent search only lasted a couple of months. The process started in February and went until May. By starting now, we’re hoping we’ll have more candidates applying for the position,” Evans told the Post.
articles.title: School district starts search for new superintendent

articles.text: During the September 9 school board meeting members of the Piedmont Education Foundation presented a check large in dimensions and sum to the school district. PEF members bestowed a record $4,355,000 check to the board to support Piedmont schools this year. It was the largest in the foundation’s history. The check pools together the efforts from every donor, volunteer, and event participant from the Giving Campaign, Spring Fling, the Harvest Festival, Dress Best for Less, business sponsors, and endowment support. For the 2026-27 school year, the PEF grant to PUSD accounts for 16% of teacher salaries, while also supporting paraeducator and teaching aides, counselors and specialists, health and wellness programs, special education, professional development and classroom supplies. “To understand the critical role of the Giving Campaign, you have to really look at what kind of funding goes to PUSD. 61% comes from the state and federal funding. Twenty-nine percent comes from parcel taxes and local fees, and that leaves a funding gap of about 10% to 9% in order to keep our schools at the excellent place that they are, so this year the gap is $2,528. That is more than it’s been ever,” explained PEF Board Member Kim Hunter. Bridget Schreiber, chair of the Education Foundation also acknowledged a grant made by a former Havens teacher. “We were also deeply moved by the continuation of a $25,000 annual professional development grant bequest from Pamela Wells Raffanelli, now in its third year of a four-year, $100,000 commitment honoring a cherished Piedmont teacher (Raffanelli) who chose to leave a legacy for Piedmont educators,” said Schreiber. While presenting the check, PEF introduced this year’s Giving Campaign chairs, Bindu Lokre, Brook Meakins, and Ellie Sommers. This year’s campaign will launch on Tuesday, September 22. To learn more about this year’s Giving Campaign and how to support Piedmont’s public schools, visit PiedmontEdFoundation.org. articles.text: It was a dramatic ending for Piedmont High in its 20-14 loss to Salesian on Friday, September 11 at Witter Field. With 13 seconds left in the game, the Pride connected the go-ahead touchdown on a 13-yard pass, where quarterback Izeah Buchanan fit a ball to the back of the end zone to receiver Sal Guerra for a leaping catch over three Highlander defenders. PHS led 7-6 by halftime and 14-6 at the start of the fourth quarter, and was in control for much of the game. However, Salesian cut the deficit to 14-12 with 7:10 left in the game before landing the game-winner. “Our defense played great, but it’s a game of a play here and there that gets you. We have a lot of injuries we’re trying to overcome, but that’s no excuse. Salesian is one of the best coached teams in the Bay Area. It’s just one of those games, we were right there,” coach Jordan Seiden said. “Salesian’s a good team. We showed we can hang with them, we just have to finish… Incredible play by their receiver, for sure. We had three people on him and he made a helluva catch. It’s one of the plays where we’ve got to get the stop, it was a coin-flip,” senior safety and receiver Diego Hurwitz reflected on the final score. Piedmont got into the red zone while leading 14-12 but couldn’t finish the drive at 4th-and-7 at the 17. They also got to Salesian’s eight early in the second quarter, but failed to convert a 4th-and-6. “We got into the red zone with three minutes left but couldn’t finish the job. Not running the right. It comes down to Salesian getting a long run near the end. It’s just little things that are fixable, but signs of a young team,” Seiden said. Still, there were a lot of bright spots for a Piedmont High team that lost to Salesian 41-17 last season and 46-14 in 2024. Sophomore quarterback Cyrus Emmanuelson got his first start of the season, completing 50 percent of his passes for 210 yards and two touchdowns. Hurwitz also logged his third touchdown of the season with 85 yards on three catches. “Frustrating loss, but I like the effort we put in tonight, we just gotta finish. I really appreciate my coaches and teammates believing in me. I’m learning what parts of the field I should attack, I really enjoy throwing over the middle right now,” Emmanuelson said. “It was a helluva game. The o-line maybe had its best game, Cyrus was dishing out passes and didn’t have a lot of pressure. We’re mastering the playbook, the more you run it, the more you execute. With our passing game, Cyrus is getting a lot better at reading defenses and knowing what to do, and when to do it,” Hurwitz said. On Piedmont’s ensuing possession, Colby Hong returned a short kickoff to the 47. articles.text: Hola from Madrid and Lisbon! In years past, the Post has taken its summer vacation abroad to Spain and Portugal, visiting some of the best sites for a day full of walking. Should you ever find yourself in Iberian Country, here are a couple of places to consider for getting your steps in. Madrid’s historic El Retiro Park Madrid makes for the perfect city to walk off all the calories from tapas. Should you ever find yourself in the Spanish Capital, make your way to Parque de El Retiro. El Retiro Park was created in 1630; it is famous for its landscape, architecture, fountains, and countless statues commemorating its past. It’s a huge park at 350 acres and a popular destination for locals and tourists alike with an estimated total of 15,000 trees. You can easily take a full day walking around the park, finding fountains, sitting areas, grassy knolls, and shaded spots to hide from the sun. Perhaps the most popular feature of El Retiro Park is the Estanque Grande de El Retiro, or the Great Pond of the park. The pond is 280 meters long, 140 meters wide, with restaurants along the edges, bands looking for tips, and boats wading around the water. Standing tall at the east edge of the Great Pond is the Monumento a Alfonso XII—the largest monument of the park. The monument is 30 meters high, 86 meters long, and 58 meters wide. At its center is the casted bronze equestrian statue of King Alfonso XII, who was the King of Spain from 1874-1885. Palacio de Cristal is one of the most popular sites of the park. With its own pond, it’s a place where many tourists will be taking selfies, or enjoying another band playing music for tips. Parque Eduardo VII to Praça do Comércio in Lisbon Portugal is considered a great city for walking and hiking. articles.text: San Francisco Opera has postponed its annual Opera Ball, the company’s largest fundraising event, following a strike by members of the San Francisco Opera Orchestra. The ball, originally scheduled for September 12 at San Francisco City Hall, will now take place Thursday, November 12. The red-carpet evening will include cocktails, dinner and dancing inside City Hall, but will no longer include an opera performance. The post ponement was announced September 1, after the orchestra said its musicians would not perform unless the opera and the orchestra reached a new collective bargaining agreement by the opening of the season. The two sides had been in negotiations over a successor agreement after their previous contract expired July 31. San Francisco Opera leadership said postponing the gala would give the negotiations more time while removing uncertainty for guests, donors and the numerous outside vendors involved in producing the event. The event had originally been planned as the opening-night celebration for the Opera’s 104th season. Guests were to begin the evening with cocktails and dinner at City Hall before crossing Van Ness Avenue to the War Memorial Opera House for a performance of Giuseppe Verdi’s Simon Boccanegra, followed by an after-party at City Hall. Instead, Opera Ball will stand on its own as a fundraising event in November. Matthew Shilvock, General Director of San Francisco Opera, said the new date would allow the gala to proceed without uncertainty surrounding the labor negotiations. “I am deeply grateful to all those involved for pivoting to this new November date, particularly the co-chairs and host committee who are working tirelessly to make this such a special fundraiser,” Shilvock said. “We feel that this is the best decision to ensure that this critical fundraising event can continue, free of any uncertainty, while at the same time giving negotiations the space needed to proceed ahead of what promises to be a beautiful opening of Simon Boccanegra on September 12. I am deeply grateful to all those attending Opera Ball for their understanding as we make this adjustment.” The orchestra strike subsequently forced the cancellation of the September 12 opening-night performance of Simon Boccanegra, as well as the annual free Opera in the Park concert scheduled for September 13. The company has since listed Simon Boccanegra performances beginning September 16 at the War Memorial Opera House. The Opera Ball has long been an important source of funding for both San Francisco Opera and the San Francisco Opera Guild. Proceeds support the Opera’s artistic programming and the Guild’s K-12 education programs. The 2026 ball was also to honor the late Diane B. Wilsey, who served as Opening Weekend Grand Sponsor for 20 years, supporting Opera Ball, the season-opening performance and Opera in the Park. The original event was to feature the opening of Verdi’s Simon Boccanegra, a political drama set in 14th-century Genoa. Music Director Eun Sun Kim was scheduled to conduct, with Mongolian baritone Amartuvshin Enkhbat in the title role, soprano Eleonora Buratto as Amelia and Maria, tenor Joshua Guerrero as Gabriele Adorno and bass-baritone Christian Van Horn as Jacopo Fiesco. For the November event, the Opera says additional details will be announced in the coming weeks. The event will be held entirely at City Hall and will not include a staged opera performance.
articles.title: SF Opera postpones annual Opera Ball amid orchestra strike

articles.text: The annual Flower Piano festival concludes Sunday, September 20, with a closing-day celebration at the San Francisco Botanical Garden in Golden Gate Park. The festival brings a dozen pianos to the garden’s 55 acres, inviting visitors to explore the grounds while listening to music among the plants and flowers. The final-day celebration at the garden’s Celebration Garden, transformed into the “Flower Piano Lounge,” runs from noon to 7:30 p.m. and features performances by Mariah Parker’s Indo Latin Jazz Ensemble, The Kevin Gerzevitz Trio and the Kev Choice Chamber Ensemble. Mariah Parker’s Indo Latin Jazz Ensemble performs from 1 to 2 p.m., followed by The Kevin Gerzevitz Trio from 3 to 4 p.m. and the Kev Choice Chamber Ensemble from 5 to 7 p.m. Throughout the festival, professional musicians and community partners perform at pianos located throughout the garden, with open-play periods allowing visitors to sit down and play themselves. The music ranges from classical and jazz to Afro-Cuban and other genres. Sunset Piano, which presents the festival in partnership with the San Francisco Botanical Garden, places grand and baby grand pianos throughout the garden each year. Visitors can bring blankets or foldable chairs for lawn seating. A limited number of chairs will also be available. General admission to Flower Piano is included with admission to the San Francisco Botanical Garden. The Flower Piano Lounge is a separate ticketed experience. Visit https://gggp.org/flowerpiano/ to purchase tickets. Kev Choice closes out this year’s festival.

The Treasure Island Museum will host a swing dance fundraiser on Saturday, September 26, to support the museum’s educational programs and historical exhibitions. The event is organized by the Treasure Island Museum Board. Live entertainment will be provided by the Nick Rossi Swing Six, a jazz and salsa ensemble specializing in music from the 1930s and 1940s. Guests will also enjoy classic cocktails from Gold Bar Distillery and a onenight-only exhibition featuring rarely displayed artifacts from the museum’s Pan American Airways collection. The museum, housed in a historic building dating to the height of the Swing Era, will serve as the backdrop for the evening’s festivities. Attendees are encouraged to wear festive or vintage-inspired attire, although period dress is not required. Prizes will be awarded for the most authentic and creative vintage outfits. Proceeds from the fundraiser will benefit the museum’s educational programming and ongoing efforts to preserve and interpret the history of Treasure Island through exhibits and public outreach. The fundraiser will take place Saturday, September 26, from 7 to 10 p.m. at the Treasure Island Museum, 39 Treasure Island Road, San Francisco. articles.text: Berkeley Repertory Theatre presents The Cook, showing onstage now through October 11. Directed by Berkeley Rep Associate Artistic Director David Mendizábal, The Cook follows an aristocratic Cuban family that flees Havana for Miami on the eve of Fidel Castro’s revolution, leaving their mansion in the care of their devoted cook, Gladys. Gladys promises to protect the home until the family returns. For 40 years, she kept her promise while enduring personal loss, political upheaval and the changing fortunes of Cuba. When the aristocrats’ daughter eventually returns, Gladys confronts the sacrifices she has made for a relationship that has been forgotten. “I’m thrilled to be bringing Eduardo Machado’s play The Cook to life at Berkeley Rep and opening our 2026/27 season with this timely play,” said Mendizábal in a press release. “A landmark work in the American theatrical canon by a Latine playwright, the play illuminates Cuba’s complex history surrounding Fidel Castro’s revolution through richly drawn characters, focusing on their Photo by Ben Krantz Daniel Duque-Estrada and Yesenia Iglesias in Eduardo Machado’s The Cook. humanity, dreams, and ambitions. It is a deeply moving story about belonging and survival and asks the question, who has the greater claim to a nation’s identity—the people who stayed or those who were forced to leave?” The cast includes Gisela Chipe as Adria/Lourdes, Daniel Duque-Estrada as Carlos, Yesenia Iglesias as Gladys, Georgina Morillo as Elena/Rosa and Ashton Muñiz as Julio. Understudies are Luis Kelly-Duarte, Morillo, Monica Rose Slater, Omar Stewart and Courtney Thomas. Machado is the playwright, with Tanya Orellana as scenic designer, Toni-Leslie James as costume designer, Mextly Couzin as lighting designer and Mikaal Sulaiman as sound designer and composer of original music. Matthew Armentrout is the wigs and hair designer, and Adi Cabral is the voice and dialect coach. The Cook runs now through Sunday, October 11. Visit https:// www.berkeleyrep.org/ to purchase tickets.

articles.text: Play ends Sept. 20 Marin Theatre opens its 60th season with the Bay Area premiere of The White Chip, a play about alcoholism and recovery, running now through September 20. Written by Sean Daniels and directed by Marin Theatre Executive Artistic Director Lance Gardner, the play follows Steven, a successful theater director whose career and personal life are increasingly affected by his struggle with alcohol addiction. articles.text: The film Pressure examines the most tense 72 hours of World War II, a stint when the weather forecasts were the most crucial piece of intelligence in the war. Directed by Anthony Maras and based on David Haig’s stage play of the same name, Pressure stars Andrew Scott and Brendan Fraser. Scott plays Captain James Stagg, a meteorologist tasked with predicting the weather to determine whether the D-Day invasion can happen at all. Brendan Fraser plays General Dwight Eisenhower, the Supreme Commander of the Allied Expeditionary Force for Western Europe and D-Day. The entire invasion hinges upon the weather report, and Scott plays that pressure with a controlled desperation that never dips into melodrama. The movie is carried through conversation in two rooms across a handful of days showing professional respect fraying under the weight of an impossible decision. The best part of the film occurs when Stagg holds his ground against men with more rank and less humility, especially Chris Messina as rival forecaster Irving Krick, a man filled with plenty of confidence and no caution. The historical details feel authentic, and the music score helps heighten the tension. The movie stumbles a bit with some historical inaccuracies. There are a few too many liberties taken with the real timeline and the real people involved. Eisenhower’s real D-Day address trimmed down for the film didn’t help either; the full speech carries more weight than what made the cut. The movie title’s double entendre speaks of pressure in both the war room and the meteorological sense. If you like historical dramas that trust dialogue over spectacle, this movie is for you. Pressure builds adequate tension, and the behind-thescenes weather reporting adds something new to a well-documented war battle. Pressure . Directed by Anthony Maras. Starring Andrew Scott, Brendan Fraser, Kerry Condon, Chris Messina, and Damian Lewis. Rated PG-13. 1h 40min. Released in 2026. Watch it now on Peacock, Amazon Prime, and AppleTV. articles.text: The first house in Piedmont was built by brothers William and Walter Blair and was on Highland Avenue (then called Vernal) between Blair Avenue and Park Way. into the Piedmont hills. articles.text: Wednesday Walkers tour homes On the hottest day of early September, about 40 hardy humans and five canine companions braved the sun, gathering at the Exedra to answer a burning real estate question: Does a home’s architect actually affect its market value? Leading the Sept. 9 Walking on Wednesday tour was Moya Robinson, a local Realtor uniquely qualified to tackle the subject. Robinson guided walkers past seven Piedmont residences designed by prominent architects, comparing their historic selling prices against average market trends. The goal was to see if architectural pedigree consistently drives a premium price—and the answer, it turns out, is nuanced. The tour focused on master builders active during Piedmont’s prime development era between 1907 and 1940. Among them was Oakland-raised Julia Morgan (1872–1957), a UC Berkeley civil engineering graduate and the first woman licensed as an architect in California. Renowned for designing Hearst Castle, Morgan crafted roughly 10 distinguished residences in Piedmont within 15 years of the city’s founding. Walkers also examined works by Albert Lincoln Farr (1871– 1947), known for Craftsman and Georgian residences, as well as civic landmarks like Piedmont City Hall, the Exedra monument, and Piedmont Community Church. Other featured architects included John Hudson Thomas (1878–1945), master of Arts & Crafts and European revival styles, and Joseph Francis Ward (1898–1970), who partnered with Farr starting in 1922. Setting out south on Highland Avenue and turning east onto Sierra Avenue, the group arrived at 12 Sierra Ave. Designed by Thomas in 1914, the Arts & Crafts home features steep rooflines, prominent gables, grouped windows, and traditional millwork. When it sold in 2008, marketing materials prominently featured Thomas’ name. Further up the street, a pair of Julia Morgan designs highlighted her architectural range. Built in 1925, 45 Sierra Ave. presents strong horizontal lines, lowpitched rooflines, broad eaves, and stucco walls—a geometric contrast to Thomas’ work. It sold in 2013 with Morgan’s name as a primary selling point. Next door, 49 Sierra Ave., constructed in 1914, displays classic Tudor influences with steep cross-gables, half-timbering, and leaded windows. Currently undergoing renovation, the house spurred discussion on how modernization—like updated wiring, roofs, kitchens, and baths—must balance with historical preservation. Morgan’s legacy was key to its 2023 sale. Ascending Mountain Avenue, the group surveyed 284 Mountain Ave., designed by Farr in 1914. The substantial Arts & Crafts estate features dramatic gables and a prominent chimney. articles.text: Antioch Court will become one of Oakland’s newest outdoor salsa destinations as Montclair Village brings a full afternoon of dancing, live DJ sets and beginner-friendly instruction to the Village Plaza as part of its popular Picnic on the Plaza series. The free event, Salsa & Sangria, is on Sunday, September 20, from noon to 4 p.m. at 2066 Antioch Court, Oakland, CA. The event will feature a professionally installed dance floor, salsa instruction from the Oakland Salsa Club, music by Dímelo DJ, and hosting by Candi Martinez. The event is designed to make salsa dancing accessible to everyone, from experienced dancers to people stepping onto a dance floor for the very first time. “Picnic on the Plaza is about creating opportunities for people to come together in the heart of Montclair Village,” said Daniel Swafford, Executive Director of the Montclair Village Association. “This event takes that idea one step further by inviting people to get up and dance together. You don’t need experience, a partner, or even fancy dance shoes—just come ready to have fun.” The afternoon kicks off with an Open Floor DJ set from noon to 1 p.m., followed by Absolute Beginner’s Salsa Lessons from 1 to 2 p.m. The afternoon culminates with a Salsa Social from 2 to 4 p.m., giving participants the chance to put their newly learned steps into action. The salsa celebration is also an opportunity to experience Montclair Village as a walkable neighborhood destination. Visitors can stop by the Sangria Bar, grab lunch, snacks, and beverages from more than 20 local restaurants and eateries, or pick up fresh food and other offerings at the Village Farmers’ Market before settling in at community tables throughout the plaza. The event also highlights the work of the Oakland Salsa Club, whose mission includes providing free dance education to historically marginalized and underserved communities in Oakland. More information about the event is on MontclairVillage.com.

articles.text: Nathan & Co celebrates 20 years in Oakland with a new home on Piedmont Avenue Nathan & Co, the Oakland-based gift and home retailer known for its colorful mix of gifts, home accessories, children’s merchandise, and locally inspired finds, is moving into a new flagship location on Piedmont Avenue, just across the street from the store it has called home for the past 18 years. Nathan & Co expects to open its new Piedmont Avenue flagship on Saturday, October 10, 2026. The move comes as Nathan & Co celebrates its 20th anniversary in Oakland. Earlier this year, owner Nathan Waldon announced that the Piedmont Avenue store would close after selling its longtime building and facing a significant increase in occupancy costs. What initially felt like the end of an era quickly turned into an unexpected new beginning when a nearby storefront became available. “We were heartbroken at the thought of leaving Piedmont Avenue,” said Waldon. “This is where Nathan & Co started 20 years ago. It’s our neighborhood, our community, and such an important part of our story. Then, almost out of nowhere, this wonderful space opened up directly across the street. It felt like the universe was telling us we weren’t finished here yet.” The new store, formerly home to Cotton Basics, is being completely refreshed and redesigned for Nathan & Co. The space will feature new lighting, fixtures, signage, a dedicated gift-wrapping area, and a warm, modern interior reflecting the retailer’s evolving aesthetic. The move also allows Nathan & Co to remain close to the customers and neighboring businesses that have supported the company since its early days. “We’ve been touched by the The company’s College Avenue store will remain open and recently underwent an exterior refresh. reaction from the neighborhood,” Waldon said. “When people thought we were leaving Piedmont Avenue, there was an enormous outpouring of love. Being able to tell everyone that we’re actually staying, and essentially moving across the street, has been one of the happiest surprises of my retail career.” Nathan & Co opened in Oakland in 2006 and has grown into a locally recognized independent retailer with locations on Piedmont Avenue and College Avenue in Rockridge. Over the years, the stores have become known for an ever-changing assortment of gifts, children’s products, home goods, jewelry, greeting cards, Oakland-inspired merchandise, and complimentary gift wrapping with a strong focus on personal customer service. “This new store brings together everything I’ve learned over many years in retail,” Waldon said. “It feels fresh and new, but it still feels completely like Nathan & Co. Most importantly, we get to begin our next 20 years right here in Oakland.” Founded in Oakland in 2006, Nathan & Co is an independent gift, home and lifestyle retailer with stores on Piedmont Avenue and College Avenue. The company offers a curated assortment of gifts, home accessories, children’s products, greeting cards, locally inspired merchandise, and unexpected finds, all presented with a distinctly Oakland point of view.

articles.text: Art was born in Jersey City, New Jersey, to working-class parents, Oscar and Ida Shartsis, in 1945. In 1949, his family moved to Los Angeles’s San Fernando Valley to chase the aerospace boom of postwar California. Art thrived: he was valedictorian of North Hollywood High School and went on to the University of California, Berkeley, which he later called the most formative experience of his life—and where he was again chosen as valedictorian, delivering the 1967 commencement speech that made national headlines. From there he went to Berkeley Law, where he met Mary Jo, and after a brief stint as an associate at Morrison & Foerster, co-founded the firm Shartsis & Friese with Bob Friese in 1975. Mary Jo joined them shortly after, leaving a more prestigious firm behind, and became one of the pioneering women in the San Francisco legal profession. Art approached his life with an intensity of purpose, pursuing excellence in everything he took on, whether it was public office, the courtroom, or representing the board of one of the world’s most valuable companies. On the board of the Bay Area Rapid Transit District, he was the leading advocate for making the system accessible to riders with disabilities. In addition to his professional accomplishments, Art will be remembered for his generous spirit and the pride he took in giving back to his communities. Some of his greatest fulfillment came from coaching Cal’s mock trial team, a commitment he kept for two decades, and Berkeley Law later honored him and Mary Jo with its highest alumni award. He found the greatest joy in the successes of those whose lives he Arthur J. Shartsis touched. Art also had a lifelong passion for photography. Early in his career he represented the photographer Imogen Cunningham, which led him to represent other prominent artists and co-found what is now California Lawyers for the Arts. His love of fly fishing led him to help found the Henry’s Fork Foundation, which continues to protect its namesake Idaho trout river to this day. In his later years he took up garden design, spending nearly two decades building the gardens that surround his Piedmont home. He also loved playing cribbage and watching his children and grandchildren’s sporting events. Art was predeceased by his wife of nearly fifty years, Mary Jo Shartsis. Later in life he married Stephanie, who shared his love of the garden and helped reshape much of it in his final years. She survives him along with his sister, Loretta Shartsis; his sons Alexander, Matthew, and Benjamin; his daughters-in-law Kim and Melanie; his grandchildren Aidan, Sophie, Fern, Hawk, and Savannah; and countless colleagues, students, and friends.
articles.title: Arthur J. Shartsis, distinguished trial lawyer, passed away at age 80

From there he went to Berkeley Law, where he met Mary Jo, and after a brief stint as an associate at Morrison & Foerster, co-founded the firm Shartsis & Friese with Bob Friese in 1975. Mary Jo joined them shortly after, leaving a more prestigious firm behind, and became one of the pioneering women in the San Francisco legal profession. Art approached his life with an intensity of purpose, pursuing excellence in everything he took on, whether it was public office, the courtroom, or representing the board of one of the world’s most valuable companies. On the board of the Bay Area Rapid Transit District, he was the leading advocate for making the system accessible to riders with disabilities. In addition to his professional accomplishments, Art will be remembered for his generous spirit and the pride he took in giving back to his communities. Some of his greatest fulfillment came from coaching Cal’s mock trial team, a commitment he kept for two decades, and Berkeley Law later honored him and Mary Jo with its highest alumni award. He found the greatest joy in the successes of those whose lives he Arthur J. Shartsis touched. Art also had a lifelong passion for photography. Early in his career he represented the photographer Imogen Cunningham, which led him to represent other prominent artists and co-found what is now California Lawyers for the Arts. His love of fly fishing led him to help found the Henry’s Fork Foundation, which continues to protect its namesake Idaho trout river to this day. In his later years he took up garden design, spending nearly two decades building the gardens that surround his Piedmont home. He also loved playing cribbage and watching his children and grandchildren’s sporting events. Art was predeceased by his wife of nearly fifty years, Mary Jo Shartsis. Later in life he married Stephanie, who shared his love of the garden and helped reshape much of it in his final years. She survives him along with his sister, Loretta Shartsis; his sons Alexander, Matthew, and Benjamin; his daughters-in-law Kim and Melanie; his grandchildren Aidan, Sophie, Fern, Hawk, and Savannah; and countless colleagues, students, and friends. Should you ever find yourself in Lisboa, an easy walk for all ages goes straight through the heart of the city from Parque Eduardo VII, down Avenida da Liberdade and Rau Augusta to the historic Praça do Comércio and edge of the Tagus River for just 2.1 miles of walking. The path nears its end down R. Augusta Avenue to the Arco da Rau Augusta. Starting at Park Eduardo VII makes it a slight downhill course to Praça do Comércio. Parque Eduardo VII is 64 acres and just north of Avenida da Liberdad. It is famous for its intricate hedge work, flanked by long walkways to the left and right. At the observation deck at the top of the park, you can see a statue of Marquês de Pombal and the Tagus River off in the distance. From there, venture down Avenida da Liberdade, a shaded and beautiful 1,100 meter avenue down the center of Lisbon. The avenue is lined with numerous monuments to several historical Portuguese figures and events. Avenida da Liberdade comes to an end at Monumento aos Restauradores (Monument to the Restorers). The route veers slightly toward the Estátua do Rei Dom Pedro IV, another town square with two fountains and the Column of Pedro IV in between. Take a tasty detour after the Monumento aos Restauradores to A Ginjinha, is an historic openfront bar that opened in 1840. That’s where you can sip Portugal’s famous cherry liquor. The location was publicized by travel journalists Anthony Bordain and Rick Steves. Head down R. Augusta Avenue where you can find several gift shops and restaurants on your way to the Arco da Rau Augusta and Commerce Square. In the center of Praça do Comércio is a monument to King José I, created in 1775. Your journey ends across the street from Commerce Square at Cais das Colunas, a pier named after the two columns on the edge of the Tagus River. articles.text: As fall begins, the Piedmont Fire Department urges residents to set aside time to complete a simple, easy-to-follow at-home wildfire evacuation exercise with their household. The exercise provides step-by-step instructions and discussion prompts in a short video that families, housemates, and neighbors can use to transform their wildfire “what ifs” into a tangible, actionable plan. The short exercise helps you spot gaps, talk through decisions, and walk away more confident about what to do if a wildfire comes. What to expect: • A realistic, local wildfire scenario based on conditions in Piedmont • Simple, pause-and-discuss prompts for each stage of • • • evacuation A downloadable worksheet to capture your household’s plan and next steps A calm, supportive narrator to walk you through the process Total time: 30-45 minutes Watch the video and download the worksheet at piedmont.ca.gov/ WildfirePlan. Find additional wildfire preparedness resources at piedmont.ca.gov/Wildfire. The at-home evacuation exercise is one part of the Piedmont Fire Department’s broader work partnering with community members to build a safer, more resilient Piedmont. Last year, the department conducted a practical evacuation drill for the Blair/Scenic/Alta neighborhood, giving residents a hands-on opportunity to test their own evacuation plans. Firefighters also provide year-round public education, coordinate training with regional partners, and offer home visits to help residents understand steps they can take to harden their properties. The department also recently led the development of Piedmont’s Local Hazard Mitigation Plan, engaging residents in a collaborative process to create a five-year roadmap that identifies steps the city can take to reduce the effects of disasters before they happen. Each household that completes the at-home exercise adds another layer of readiness to these efforts – strengthening not just their own plans, but our community’s resilience as a whole.

I am left to wonder when, having invested so heavily in the weapons of war, we invest in the work of beating swords into plowshares, spears into pruning hooks? When do we prioritize restoration over revenge? I know the word is misused, misapplied and misunderstood, yet, I would suggest that at some point we need to get serious about forgiveness. I would argue that to escape the cycle of toxic animosity that grips us, we must forgive, we must release those who have done us wrong from the debt they owe. I would suggest that unless we want to forever worship at the altar of the God named “Get Even,” we need to apply the teaching of Jesus that forgiving “seventy times seven” is the only path to enduring peace. In some ways it is easier to call for forgiveness at an international level than it is to practice it in our communities, our congregations and our personal lives. Yet, if forgiveness is not a personal practice, it is hypocritical to suggest that it is a path to world peace. Thus, let me end with the invitation for each of us to consider who it is that we need to forgive and how it is we need to be forgiven and then, before too much time goes by, put the words “I am sorry” and “You are forgiven” to use and in our own way, seek to heal rather than to punish. Jim Hopkins in Pastor Emeritus of Lakeshore Avenue Baptist Church in Oakland.
